issues.item: Compulsive Exercise: I push myself to exercise excessively
issues.explanation: The maladaptive strategies cluster is not well anchored to the rest of the profile. Excessive exercise and alcohol use can occur in PTSD, but in this profile they are hard to connect to the dominant threat-memory pattern centered on danger vigilance after a motor vehicle collision. With no trigger links active, these strategies should still fit the patient’s central formulation via memory/threat/appraisals, yet these two items feel relatively generic and not clearly tied to the reported intrusive reliving, vigilance, and environmental scanning.

Dehumanization is the main inconsistent appraisal. Feeling like an object is more characteristic of interpersonal trauma involving humiliation, coercion, or abuse than a life-threatening motor vehicle collision. It also sits awkwardly beside the rest of the profile, which is strongly organized around danger anticipation, distrust, and reliving of the crash. In contrast, shame on recall plus dehumanization suggests a different trauma meaning that is not otherwise represented in the memory, threat, or strategy items.

issues.item: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, intense shame on recall is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly supported by the rest of the content. The other memory items emphasize sensory reliving and replay, while no appraisal item directly explains shame about the event (e.g. self-blame, humiliation, permanent damage). This makes the shame item clinically hard to integrate with the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person
issues.explanation: 'I feel like an object, not like a person' is more characteristic of interpersonal trauma, coercion, or dehumanizing abuse than a motor vehicle collision. In this profile there are no companion items about bodily violation, humiliation, or identity damage that would make this appraisal cohere after an MVC.

issues.item: Distrust Others: People are not what they seem
issues.explanation: 'People are not what they seem' implies a generalized interpersonal mistrust. For an MVC profile dominated by danger scanning and reliving, that belief is possible but is not well anchored by the trauma type or by other selected items, which focus on environmental threat rather than betrayal or intentional human threat. This creates a cross-node mismatch in the formulation content.

issues.item: Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma
issues.explanation: This item is the main coherence problem. For a 24-year-old female survivor of a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, the rest of the profile is tightly organized around fear-based PTSD: hypervigilant threat monitoring, danger-focused appraisals, and highly sensory reliving memory. 'Seeking Conflict' reflects an externalizing/drama-generating coping style that is not supported by the other selected items and does not fit the predominant cognitive formulation as well as the other strategies do. Alcohol use and checking surroundings plausibly connect to threat and memory, but picking arguments to distract herself pulls toward a different presentation and is hard to explain from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Alcohol Use: drink alcohol
issues.explanation: Alcohol use is not impossible, but in this profile it is weakly integrated with the rest of the selected content. The other items depict a tightly fear-based, hypervigilant motor-vehicle-collision presentation focused on environmental scanning, sleep vigilance, back-to-wall positioning, reliving, and danger-based appraisals. A solitary alcohol-use item without any parallel avoidance/numbing/interpersonal dysregulation content makes the coping pattern feel clinically disconnected from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
issues.explanation: For a life-threatening motor vehicle collision, generalized scanning for threat is coherent, but specifically 'noticing weapons' pulls toward assault/interpersonal violence content. Given that the rest of the profile is entirely accident-based and contains no interpersonal-threat, attack, or weapon-related memory/appraisal material, this item is difficult to reconcile with the otherwise coherent accident formulation.

vignette:
Leila was twenty-two years old, working as a tailor in a small shop in a suburban strip mall, when the collision happened. She had been driving home after a late shift, the autumn dusk settling fast, when a pickup truck ran a red light and T-boned her driver’s side door. She remembered the sound—metal crumpling, glass exploding inward—and the sensation of the car spinning, then the world tilting as her vehicle came to rest against a lamppost. Her left arm was pinned against the shattered door; blood pooled in her lap from a gash on her forehead. For what felt like minutes, she was certain she was going to die. Firemen had to pry the door open. At the hospital, they told her she had a concussion, three broken ribs, and deep lacerations, but she would recover. What the doctors did not see was that the collision had planted something in her that would not heal with stitches or time.

Now, two years later at twenty-four, Leila still could not bring herself to sit in a car. The thought of being inside any vehicle—even as a passenger—sent her heart racing so hard she felt dizzy. Her mother had offered to drive her to work in the months after the accident, but Leila refused, walking over an hour each way through the busy streets of her neighborhood. She told herself it was just until she felt ready, but the readiness never came. Instead, the walking gave her a false sense of control: she could see threats coming, she could dart into a doorway if a car swerved too close. She began scanning every intersection, every driver’s face, every approaching headlight. At work, she chose the back corner of the tailor shop, positioning her sewing table so her back was against the wall. From that spot she could see the entire room—the front door, the fitting mirrors, the rack of garments. When customers entered, she watched their hands, their posture, the way they moved. Her boss asked if she was feeling all right; she said she was just being careful.

But the carefulness grew into a constant, exhausting vigilance that had not eased in two years. Leila found herself mentally rehearsing disasters in any setting. On the walk to work, she would picture a speeding car jumping the curb and plan how she would throw herself sideways. In the shop, she imagined a robber bursting in and practiced which scissors were within reach to defend herself. At night, lying in her studio apartment, she could not relax enough to fall asleep. Her bed was against the wall, and she faced the door, her back pressed to the headboard. She kept a small lamp on, telling herself it was for safety. But the only thing the light did was illuminate the fear: the memory of the collision would replay unbidden, always exactly the same—the sound, the spin, the certainty of death. When it came, she felt the same terror flooding her body, as if she were still trapped in the wreck. She would sit up, heart pounding, unable to convince herself it was over.

The world had become a place of hidden dangers. Leila began to distrust strangers; she believed that no one revealed their true intentions. On the street, when a man glanced at her, she interpreted it as predatory. When a car slowed nearby, she prepared for an attack. She told herself that this hypervigilance was necessary—that the collision had taught her a harsh lesson: she had to be ready for the next catastrophe, because it would come without warning. The only way to survive was to stay vigilant every second. Yet the irony was that she was not surviving; she was merely existing inside a fortress of dread. Her relationships frayed. She canceled plans with friends because she could not face the idea of riding in their cars. They stopped inviting her. Her mother grew frustrated, saying Leila was “too on edge” and needed to let go. Leila felt misunderstood; how could she let go when the film in her head kept playing? She had not taken a single drive since the accident. Her life had shrunk to the walk-to-work, the corner of the tailor shop, the wall behind her bed.

What finally brought her to seek help, at twenty-four, was a morning when she stood at the shop’s front door, unable to turn the handle. She had scanned the street for ten minutes, certain that a truck was about to crash through the window. Her hands were shaking. Her boss saw her through the glass and looked worried. Leila realized she could no longer pretend this was caution. She was trapped. She called a therapist the next day, afraid that if she did not, she would lose everything—her job, her freedom, her sanity. She hoped for something she could barely name: to stop the replay, to walk through a day without rehearsing her own death, to believe, just once, that the next moment might bring something other than disaster.
